## Proof

**Yes**, $P(x)$ must be the square of a polynomial with real coefficients.

**Degree constraint.** Let $n = \deg P$ and $m = \deg Q$. Then $n^2 = 2m$, so $n$ is even. If $P$ is constant, say $P = c$, then $c = Q^2 \geq 0$ and $P = (\sqrt{c})^2$, done. Hence assume $n \geq 2$.

**Factorization over $\mathbb{C}$.** Write $P(x) = a\prod_{j=1}^{s}(x - \gamma_j)^{r_j}$ where $\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_s$ are the distinct roots of $P$ (in $\mathbb{C}$) with multiplicities $r_j$, and $a \in \mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is the leading coefficient. Then

$$P(P(x)) = a\prod_{j=1}^{s}\bigl(P(x) - \gamma_j\bigr)^{r_j} = Q(x)^2.$$

**Coprimality.** For $i \neq j$, any common root $\alpha$ of $P(x)-\gamma_i$ and $P(x)-\gamma_j$ would satisfy $\gamma_i = P(\alpha) = \gamma_j$, a contradiction. So the polynomials $P(x)-\gamma_j$ are pairwise coprime.

**Consequence of the perfect-square condition.** Since $a\prod_j (P(x)-\gamma_j)^{r_j}$ is a perfect square in $\mathbb{C}[x]$ and the factors are pairwise coprime, for every $j$ with $r_j$ **odd**, the polynomial $P(x) - \gamma_j$ must itself be a perfect square in $\mathbb{C}[x]$.

**Non-real roots cannot have odd multiplicity.** Suppose $\gamma_j$ is non-real and $r_j$ is odd. Then $P(x) - \gamma_j = S_j(x)^2$ for some $S_j \in \mathbb{C}[x]$, giving $P(x) = S_j(x)^2 + \gamma_j$. Substituting:

$$P(P(x)) = S_j(P(x))^2 + \gamma_j = Q(x)^2,$$

so $(Q(x) - S_j(P(x)))(Q(x) + S_j(P(x))) = \gamma_j \neq 0$. Both factors are nonzero constants, forcing $Q$ to be constant—contradicting $\deg Q = n^2/2 \geq 2$. Hence **every non-real root of $P$ has even multiplicity**.

**Real roots with odd multiplicity force $P$ to be a square.** Suppose $\gamma$ is a real root of $P$ with odd multiplicity. Then $P(x) - \gamma$ has real coefficients and is a perfect square in $\mathbb{C}[x]$, so either:

- **Case A:** $P(x) - \gamma = S(x)^2$ for some $S \in \mathbb{R}[x]$. Then $P(x) = S(x)^2 + \gamma$ and
$$P(P(x)) = S(P(x))^2 + \gamma = Q(x)^2 \implies (Q - S\circ P)(Q + S\circ P) = \gamma.$$
If $\gamma \neq 0$, both factors are constants, forcing $Q$ constant—contradiction. So $\gamma = 0$ and $P(x) = S(x)^2$, a perfect square.

- **Case B:** $P(x) - \gamma = -T(x)^2$ for some $T \in \mathbb{R}[x]$. Then $P(x) = -T(x)^2 + \gamma$ and
$$Q(x)^2 + T(P(x))^2 = \gamma \quad\text{(a constant)}.$$
The leading coefficient of $Q^2 + (T\circ P)^2$ is a sum of squares of real numbers (both non-negative, at least one positive), hence positive—contradicting the right side being constant (degree 0) unless $Q = 0$ and $T = 0$. Then $P = \gamma = 0 = 0^2$, a perfect square.

In both cases, $P$ is a perfect square.

**All roots even multiplicity.** If no root of $P$ has odd multiplicity, then all $r_j$ are even, so $P(x) = a \cdot R(x)^2$ for some $R \in \mathbb{R}[x]$. Then

$$P(P(x)) = a \cdot R(P(x))^2 = Q(x)^2.$$

Comparing leading coefficients: $(\text{lead}\, Q)^2 = a \cdot (\text{lead}(R\circ P))^2$. The right side has sign equal to $\operatorname{sgn}(a)$, while the left side is positive. Hence $a > 0$, and

$$P(x) = \bigl(\sqrt{a}\, R(x)\bigr)^2,$$

a perfect square of a real polynomial.

**Conclusion.** In every case—whether $P$ has a real root of odd multiplicity (forcing $P = S^2$ or $P = 0$), or all roots have even multiplicity (forcing $P = (\sqrt{a}\,R)^2$ with $a > 0$)—the polynomial $P(x)$ is the square of a polynomial with real coefficients. $\blacksquare$
